ABSTRACT

Modern personal and household financial management suffers from systemic fragmentation, computational imprecision, and a lack of actionable optimization. Most consumer applications either treat users as isolated individuals or rely on floating-point approximations that introduce rounding drift into multi-party balance reconciliations. Furthermore, existing commercial platforms offer descriptive expense summaries without counterfactual optimization or empirical validation against large-scale transactional benchmarks.

This report presents the complete architectural, database, and algorithmic design of Expenzo, an enterprise-grade fintech web application engineered to solve individual and family financial coordination. Expenzo enforces mathematical accounting guarantees by operating on 64-bit integer minor units (paise and cents), eliminating IEEE-754 floating-point drift. The architecture features a decoupled, multi-tier topology comprising a modern React 18, TypeScript 5.5, and Zustand 4.5 client-state engine synchronized with a Supabase PostgreSQL 15.8 relational backend governed by 27 normalized tables and cryptographic Row-Level Security (RLS) policies.

To bridge academic research and real-world fintech deployment, Expenzo incorporates an offline streaming data ingestion pipeline capable of parsing 24.38 million IBM credit card transactions at a verified throughput of 256,441 records per second. An 18-year longitudinal cohort of 80,977 verified transactions ($5,359,206.57 USD / ₹44.48 Cr INR) across four multi-generational users is fully integrated into the application. This empirical cohort directly powers four intelligence capabilities: (1) a multi-dimensional Transaction Intelligence Explorer; (2) a counterfactual Financial Optimization Engine with Pareto discretionary truncation unlocking $224,942.50 in annual surplus; (3) a Seat-Based Family Plan Subscription Optimizer modeling 52–65% cost reductions; and (4) multi-window rolling Z-score anomaly detection identifying 7 trailing volatility spikes.

The implementation is verified through 26 automated test suites comprising 234 passing unit, integration, and accounting invariant test cases with zero failures. This document fulfills all seven criteria of Sharda University CSCR2600 Rubric 1 (Project Design Approval).

Keywords: Financial Technology (Fintech); Personal Finance Management (PFM); Multi-Tenant Architecture; Integer Minor-Unit Accounting; Family Workspace; Seat-Based Subscription Optimization; IBM Synthetic Transactions Dataset; Streaming Ingestion; Vitest; Supabase Row-Level Security.

CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION & PROBLEM FORMULATION

1.1 Context and Real-World Financial Challenges

In modern economic households, managing personal and familial financial obligations has evolved from simple checkbook balancing into an increasingly intricate, multi-channel operational endeavor. Contemporary consumers engage with an average of four to seven distinct financial instruments, including checking accounts, multiple credit card lines with disparate reward schedules, high-yield savings pots, automated investment portfolios, and digital mobile payment wallets. This proliferation of decentralized payment methods creates acute financial fragmentation.

Financial fragmentation obscures total household net worth and distorts discretionary cash flow visibility. Consumers frequently experience cognitive friction when attempting to track recurring subscriptions, resulting in silent subscription creep where unused streaming, cloud storage, and gym services silently drain monthly liquidity. When family members attempt to co-manage shared domestic expenditures—such as household groceries, utility bills, educational fees, and pooled streaming subscriptions—they are forced to rely on disconnected messaging chats, manual spreadsheet entries, or rudimentary third-party splitting utilities. These manual mechanisms lack real-time synchronization with primary banking ledgers and fail to provide holistic balance sheets.

1.2 Problem Statement & Motivation

Current personal financial management (PFM) applications suffer from four foundational engineering deficiencies:

  • 1. Numerical Imprecision and Floating-Point Drift: Most consumer financial web applications implement monetary arithmetic using standard IEEE-754 binary floating-point numbers. In multi-transaction ledgers involving thousands of entries, decimal approximations introduce cumulative rounding errors (e.g., 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004). This violates double-entry bookkeeping guarantees and creates balance reconciliation discrepancies between client dashboards and database ledgers.
  • 2. Individual-Centric Siloed Architecture: The vast majority of PFM platforms (e.g., Mint, Monarch, YNAB) model users strictly as isolated autonomous entities. They lack native primitives for family workspaces, joint savings goals, role-based visibility controls, and seat-based subscription pooling. Consequently, domestic partners are unable to view consolidated household cash flows without entirely sacrificing personal transactional privacy.
  • 3. Descriptive Rather Than Counterfactual Intelligence: Existing dashboards limit their analytical output to descriptive backwards-looking pie charts. They inform users where money was spent but fail to simulate counterfactual optimization scenarios—such as evaluating how truncating discretionary spend by 25% or consolidating high-frequency micro-charges would accelerate long-term capital accumulation.
  • 4. Absence of Large-Scale Empirical Validation: Consumer apps are rarely benchmarked against multi-year longitudinal transaction datasets. Developers test their systems on small, handcrafted mock fixtures, failing to validate system performance against real-world transactional entropy, long-term category drift, and macroeconomic seasonality.

1.3 Project Vision, Core Value Proposition & Key Differentiators

Expenzo is engineered from the ground up as a unified, enterprise-grade personal and family financial intelligence platform. Its core architectural premise is that financial software must provide deterministic accounting guarantees, end-to-end multi-user workspace isolation, and actionable algorithmic intelligence derived from massive empirical transaction datasets.

CHAPTER 2: LITERATURE REVIEW & EXISTING FINANCIAL SYSTEMS

The digitization of household financial accounting originated in early desktop software during the late 1980s, exemplified by Intuit Quicken and Microsoft Money. In behavioral finance literature, Thaler (1985, 1999) established the Theory of Mental Accounting, demonstrating that individuals categorize money into non-fungible mental accounts (e.g., entertainment, food, emergency savings), leading to suboptimal financial choices when budgets lack flexible cross-category liquidity.
